newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Sainsbury profits to slip again.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Sainsbury profits to slip again.

text.p: Britain's biggest supermarket group J. Sainsbury Plc heads for another set of disappointing results at the half year when it reports on Wednesday and will struggle to show its fortunes are turning, analysts said.

"It is like a supertanker and it is not going to spin round that quickly. But we would like to see at least that it is stopping or even slowing its voyage in the wrong direction," said one sector analyst who asked not to be named.
Sainsbury was toppled off the lead slot of supermarkets in terms of market share late last year by arch-rival Tesco.
And although its turnover checked in at a huge 13.5 billion stg last year, profits fell for the first time in 22 years.
At the half year, analysts are expecting figures to be down again, with forecasts for pretax profits of 383 to 396 million stg compared with 450 million stg previously.

But the company should edge up the dividend to around 3.5 pence per share from 3.4 pence per share as "an expression of confidence in the turnaround," said Dave Stoddart, analyst at Henderson Crosthwaite.
Attention will focus on sales figures, to see if the Reward loyalty card is boosting turnover -- or at least covering costs.
Sainsbury was forced into launching the card in June after the success of ClubCard helped to put Tesco in the top slot.
At the time, Sainsbury said it expected an uplift of around three percent in sales from the card, which would cover costs.
"The market is clearly saying it does not think they have achieved that," Stoddart said.
Speculation surfaced again on Friday that Sainsbury might announce an addition to the Reward card, such as a credit or debit card, with its results but the company would not immediately comment.
Sainsbury shares were trading at around 356 pence by 1314 GMT, up six pence, but had earlier touched down to 347 pence, just a whisker off a year low of 344 pence.

Analysts suggested the retailer, which also has Homebase do-it-yourself chain and Giant in the U.S., would need to see an increase of more than five percent in sales to cover Reward costs and increased marketing and personnel spend.
"There's nothing wrong with DIY and the U.S. is forging ahead but that's only about 10 percent operating profit," said the sector analyst.
"They just don't seem to have solved the problems with the supermarkets," he added.

Sainsbury has been trying to promote its image as a high quality, value-for-money family retailer but has lost ground to the innovative Tesco and ASDA, where the ground-breaking management has made the company a stock market favourite.
Sainsbury, which is struggling to maintain market confidence in its management team, will be expected to show the second half can be stronger, analysts said.

"There is only so long that management is going to be given the benefit of the doubt. The market needs something to hang its hat on and continuing lacklustre sales will not give that," the sector analyst said.
